newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FORECAST - HUNGARY SHARES' APPEAL TO SHRINK - NOMURA.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - HUNGARY SHARES' APPEAL TO SHRINK - NOMURA.

text.p: Hungary will remain a core market for foreign share investors in eastern Europe, but the percentage of invested assets allocated to the country is likely to drop, London-based Nomura Research said on Wednesday.
"Investors put new money into larger, cheaper markets," Nomura analyst Frances Cloud told an international conference about Hungarian capital markets.
The BUX index of the Budapest Stock Exchange (BSE) more than doubled this year, but Cloud said there were limiting factors to further rises.
Many Hungarian shares already had high valuation and the relatively low capitalisation of the Hungarian market was not likely to increase substantially in the near future, she said.
Cloud said the capitalisation of the BSE totalled only $4.6 billion, and the possible privatisation issues in the next two year could only add maximum $3 billion.
"Even after these issues, the market will remain small, Nomura said in a statement released at the conference.

8Cloud added that private company listings in Hungary were not likely to boost the BSE's capitalisation as the need of private firms for equity financing was declining and they did not wish to publish more information about themselves.

She said the Hungarian share market was likely to continue to be dominated by foreign investors in the next two or three years, who will probably choose London's SEAQ instead of the BSE in an increasing number.

Most of the trading in Hungarian shares is going through the SEAQ and the analyst said that the role of London was likely to strengthen as the importance of U.S. investors was increasing on Hungary's capital markets.
"Currently about half of the money coming to the BSE is from the U.S., and that's much more than earlier," she said. "Some 30 percent of the free float is in U.S. hands."
The trend towards trading SEAQ stocks in London will continue as the new U.S. investors required good liquidity and the best execution from the market they traded on, Nomura said.

The role of domestic investors was not likely to increase in Hungary in the short term as it did not plan mass privatisation, bank accounts offered relatively high returns and Hungarians have not discovered the attractions of capital investments, Cloud said.
However, she added that the planned reform of the social security system, which was likely to help the spread of private pension funds, may increase domestic demand for Hungarian shares.

Cloud said the Hungarian capital market was likely to remain important in the region as the country's econgmy showed signs of imprgvement, bourse companies usually had high quality and accounting standards remained the best in the region.
